subject: feminism
title: The Garden of Hope Foundation (勵馨基金會): from one halfway house to Taiwan's largest gender-violence service network
dek: Garden of Hope began in 1988 as a small Christian shelter for girls pulled out of forced prostitution. Today it runs more than fifty service sites, spends over NT$570 million a year, and gets almost half of its income from government contracts. This first lesson in the Taiwan organization series explains its history, what it actually does, how the money works, and how Taiwan's charity laws let you check any partner's books before cool dairy gives it a single dollar.
era: 1986 to the present: the anti-child-prostitution campaigns of the late 1980s, the 1995 Child and Youth Sexual Transaction Prevention Act, the 2006 Charity Donations Destined for Public Welfare Act, the 2018 Foundations Act, and the 2025 annual report
honesty: This lesson is text only. The history comes from Garden of Hope's own About page and its 2025 annual report, plus the Chinese Wikipedia articles on the foundation and on the Huaxi Street marches. All money and service figures are copied from the 2025 annual report published in April 2026, and the percentages are the report's own. The legal rules are quoted from the official texts on the Ministry of Justice law database. Where the only source is the foundation describing itself, the lesson says so. This is a study guide, not legal or financial advice: before cool dairy signs a partnership, confirm the details with the partner organization and, if needed, an accountant.

timeline.label: The Rainbow Project starts
timeline.detail: Liao Pi-ying (廖碧英), head of the Presbyterian Church in Taiwan's Rainbow women's ministry centre, investigates child prostitution in Taipei's Huaxi Street and starts the Rainbow Project (彩虹專案) to rescue girls, many of them Indigenous.

timeline.label: First Huaxi Street march
timeline.detail: On 10 January 1987 more than thirty civic groups march and sit in at Longshan Temple and Huaxi Street to protest the trafficking of girls into prostitution. Martial law is lifted in July of the same year.

timeline.label: Second march and the founding of Garden of Hope
timeline.detail: A second Huaxi Street march takes place on 9 January 1988. The same year a group of Christians, led according to Chinese Wikipedia by the American missionary Angie Golmon (高愛琪), found Garden of Hope and open what the foundation calls Taiwan's first halfway house for girls, 勵馨園.

timeline.label: The anti-child-prostitution campaign
timeline.detail: Garden of Hope organizes the 'anti-child-prostitution Huaxi Street run' and drafts a civil-society version of a law against the commercial sexual exploitation of children.

timeline.label: Child and Youth Sexual Transaction Prevention Act
timeline.detail: The act is promulgated on 11 August 1995. Garden of Hope counts it as its first major legislative victory.

timeline.label: Protecting girls nationwide
timeline.detail: The foundation builds a national 'girls' hope network' and opens the Dandelion Counseling Centre (蒲公英治療中心) for survivors of sexual assault and the people close to them.

timeline.label: Charity fundraising law
timeline.detail: The Charity Donations Destined for Public Welfare Act (公益勸募條例) is promulgated on 17 May 2006. It sets permits, receipt rules, a cap on fundraising costs, and public reporting for every public appeal.

timeline.label: Social enterprises begin
timeline.detail: Garden of Hope opens its first social enterprises, including the Sweetheart Workshop (甜心工坊) bakery, to train and employ women leaving violence.

timeline.label: The law is renamed
timeline.detail: The 1995 act is rewritten and renamed the Child and Youth Sexual Exploitation Prevention Act (兒童及少年性剝削防制條例) on 4 February 2015, taking effect on 1 January 2017.

timeline.label: The Foundations Act
timeline.detail: The Foundations Act (財團法人法) is promulgated on 1 August 2018 and takes effect six months later. It requires foundations to publish their plans, budgets, reports and financial statements.

timeline.label: Thirty years of the child-exploitation law
timeline.detail: Garden of Hope serves 20,110 children, young people and women, launches a second legal-support team for #MeToo survivors who are sued for speaking out, and marks the thirtieth anniversary of the 1995 law.

sections.title: Before Garden of Hope: girls for sale on Huaxi Street

blocks.text: In the 1980s Huaxi Street in Taipei's Wanhua district was one of the city's best-known red-light districts. Reports from church workers and journalists described girls in their early teens, many from Indigenous mountain villages, who had been sold or tricked into brothels by traffickers. Protesters accused the police and the government of tolerating the trade.

Liao Pi-ying, who ran the Presbyterian Church in Taiwan's Rainbow women's ministry centre, investigated the problem and in 1986 started the Rainbow Project to rescue girls. On 10 January 1987 more than thirty civic groups marched through Longshan Temple and Huaxi Street. The conveners listed for the marches were Liao Pi-ying, Shen Mei-chen and Tsao Ai-lan of the Awakening Foundation, and the commander on the street both years was the Atayal activist Payen Talu (巴燕·達魯) of the Alliance of Taiwan Aborigines. In August 1987 Tsao, Shen and Liao also helped found the Taiwan Women's Rescue Association, today the Taipei Women's Rescue Foundation (婦女救援基金會), one of the nine organizations on your orgs page. Their slogans attacked the customers rather than the girls: 'buying a child prostitute is a crime', and 'the customer is more shameful than the prostitute'. A second march followed on 9 January 1988 because, the organizers said, a police crackdown announced after the first march had changed little.

Historians of the Taiwan women's movement treat these marches as a turning point. Before them, newspapers mostly reported on women's groups negatively. The child-prostitution campaign was the first women's cause that won broad public sympathy, and it pushed the government toward new child-welfare laws. Martial law ended in July 1987, between the two marches, which made street protest far less dangerous than it had been when Annette Lu was jailed after the Kaohsiung Incident in 1979.

sections.title: 1988: a house for girls who had nowhere to go

blocks.text: Rescuing a girl from a brothel solved only half the problem. Many of the girls could not go home, because home was where they had been sold. Garden of Hope was founded in 1988 to answer that second question. The foundation's own history says that a group of Christians who were worried about the trafficking of girls set up Taiwan's first halfway house, called 勵馨園, to give rescued girls a place to live. Chinese Wikipedia names the American missionary Angie Golmon (高愛琪) as the founder.

Garden of Hope is still openly Christian. Its mission statement says it works 'in the spirit of Christian love and justice' to prevent and end the harm of gender-based violence. That religious root has not made it socially conservative on every issue. Its former chief executive Ji Hui-jung (紀惠容) published an article arguing that putting same-sex issues to a referendum violated human rights, and the foundation supports LGBTQ+ rights campaigns. It has, however, opposed the legalization of prostitution, including during Taiwan's 2009 debate over legal red-light zones.

sections.title: Five stages, in the foundation's own words

blocks.text: Garden of Hope divides its history into five stages. This structure comes from the organization itself, so read it as its own story about itself, but each stage matches a documented change in what it does.

items: Halfway house, 1988–1992. Shelter and care for girls rescued from prostitution.

The anti-child-prostitution movement, 1992–1995. Public campaigns such as the Huaxi Street run, and a civil-society draft of the law that became the 1995 Child and Youth Sexual Transaction Prevention Act. The act was renamed the Child and Youth Sexual Exploitation Prevention Act in 2015 and widened to cover sexual images and online exploitation.
Protecting girls, 1995–2001. A national girls' hope network and the Dandelion Counseling Centre for survivors of sexual assault.
Empowering girls and women, 2001–2008. More advocacy, and job-readiness programmes for women leaving violence.

Gender justice, 2008 to the present. Work on all forms of gender-based violence, membership of international anti-violence campaigns, and the founding of the Asian Network of Women's Shelters (ANWS), which Garden of Hope says it called together.

blocks.text: The important shift is the one from rescue to services. An organization that began with a few girls in one house now handles domestic violence, sexual violence, teenage pregnancy, family court support, migrant women and stalking. It is no longer a protest group in the way that the Awakening Foundation is. It is a large service provider that also lobbies.

sections.title: What Garden of Hope does today

blocks.text: According to its About page, Garden of Hope has more than fifty service sites in fifteen cities and counties, from Taipei to Taitung and Hualien. Its 2025 annual report, published in April 2026, gives these figures for the year 2025.

items: 20,110 children, young people and women served, and 213,565 service sessions, which include social work, legal advice, medical help and counseling.

Domestic and intimate-partner violence services in eleven branch offices under government contracts, three government-commissioned emergency short-term shelters, and family-violence service desks inside seven district courts.
Sexual violence services, including counseling for survivors and help with removing sexual images from the internet.

Residential care for girls who cannot live at home (少女安置服務): 54 girls served in 2025 across five homes in Taipei, New Taipei, Taichung, Nantou and Kaohsiung (6,227 sessions / 13,822 person-days). The foundation also counts sixteen homes in total for women and girls.

Economic empowerment for women. Among women in its economic programme, the report says average annual income rose from NT$62,247 when they joined to NT$182,339 when their case closed, and 52 percent reached stable employment.
151 advocacy actions (meetings, press conferences and visits to legislators) and 1,327 public education talks in schools, companies and government offices.
An average of 549 paid staff during the year.

blocks.text: These outcome numbers are reported by the foundation about its own clients, so they are self-assessment rather than independent evaluation. They are still useful, because a partner that measures and publishes its results is easier to hold to account than one that only tells stories.

Its current advocacy, as listed in the 2025 report, includes abolishing the statute of limitations for sexual offences against children, strengthening the Stalking and Harassment Prevention Act after three years in force (for example by adding an emergency protection order), and a legal-support team for survivors who were sued for defamation after speaking out in Taiwan's 2023 #MeToo wave.

sections.title: Where the money comes from and where it goes

blocks.text: The 2025 annual report includes a one-page financial summary. Total income was NT$640,684,355 and total spending was NT$572,457,782, leaving a surplus of NT$68,226,573 (NT$54,985,532 after capital spending). The income came from these sources.

items: Government grants and commissioned contracts: NT$305,182,872, or 47.64 percent.
Donations: NT$271,479,071, or 42.37 percent.
Service income: NT$30,763,699, or 4.8 percent.
Sales of goods and services, such as the social enterprises: NT$15,180,191, or 2.37 percent.
Other income: NT$14,863,626, or 2.32 percent.
Income of affiliated operations: NT$3,214,896, or 0.5 percent.

blocks.text: Spending went to women's services (33.15 percent), children's and youth services (22.43 percent), shelter and residential care (20.47 percent), administration (18.44 percent), community services (2.95 percent) and counseling (2.56 percent).

Two things stand out. First, almost half of the money comes from the government. In Taiwan, local governments often contract out protective services such as shelters and domestic-violence case management to private foundations. This gives Garden of Hope stable funding and a large footprint, but it also means that a lot of its work is defined by government contracts, and contract rates do not always cover the real cost. In 2017, for example, Garden of Hope joined a press conference arguing that the new 'one fixed day off and one flexible rest day' labour rule (一例一休) raised costs for social-welfare groups without matching increases in government funding; some front-line social workers answered that managers were asking underpaid staff to sacrifice in the name of charity. Second, donations are the other big pillar, which is exactly where a partner like cool dairy would fit.

The administration share of about 18 percent sounds high to many donors, but a large service organization needs accountants, auditors, IT and training, and the legal cost cap described below applies to each permitted fundraising appeal, not to the organization's whole budget. A better question than 'how low is the overhead' is whether money given for a specific project is spent on that project and reported publicly. Taiwan's laws make that question answerable.

sections.title: How Taiwan's charity laws let you check a partner

blocks.text: Two laws matter most for anyone who wants to give money to a Taiwanese women's organization: the Charity Donations Destined for Public Welfare Act of 2006 (公益勸募條例) and the Foundations Act of 2018 (財團法人法). Garden of Hope is a foundation (財團法人), so both apply to it.
The Charity Donations Destined for Public Welfare Act governs public fundraising appeals. Its main rules are these:

items: Who may run a public appeal (Article 5): public schools, administrative corporations, public-interest associations and foundations. Other people and companies cannot launch one themselves.

Permit (Article 7): each appeal needs a permit from the local government, or from the Ministry of Health and Welfare if it covers more than one city or county, and it may last at most one year (Article 12).
Receipts (Article 16): every receipt must show the permit number, the donor, the amount and the date.
Cost cap (Article 17): the costs of running an appeal may be paid from the money raised only up to 15 percent if it raises NT$10 million or less, with lower percentages above that.

Reporting (Articles 18 and 20): within thirty days after the appeal ends, the group must publish the donors and the amount raised, and within thirty days after the money is spent it must publish how it was used, after board approval, and file the report with the regulator.
Purpose (Article 19): money raised must be used according to the approved plan and may not be moved to other purposes.

blocks.text: The Foundations Act covers the organization as a whole. Article 24 requires larger foundations to have internal controls and audited financial statements and to adopt an integrity code. Article 25 requires every foundation to send its annual work plan and budget to the regulator within a month of the start of the year, and its work report and financial statements within five months of the end of the year, and to publish them within a month after the regulator receives them, together with a list of grants and donations received. Garden of Hope's About page links to exactly these documents for 2023 to 2026, including an accountant's audit report, and its donation-verification page (徵信) lists donors, in-kind gifts and the results of each permitted appeal.

For cool dairy this has a practical meaning. A shop that sells clothes and gives part of its proceeds to a foundation is normally acting as a donor, not running its own public appeal, but how cool dairy words its promises to customers still matters. Before launching, it is worth asking the partner how it will receipt the donation, whether it will appear in the partner's published donor list, and how it will report what the money paid for.

sections.title: What was happening elsewhere at the same time

blocks.text: Garden of Hope was part of a wave of East and Southeast Asian groups in the 1980s that turned the trafficking of women and girls into a public issue.

items: Japan, 1986. The Japan Woman's Christian Temperance Union opened HELP (女性の家HELP) in Tokyo to mark its centenary, mainly to shelter foreign women who were victims of human trafficking. Like Garden of Hope it came from a Christian women's tradition and moved from rescue to a broader shelter for women and children.

South Korea, 1983. The Korea Women's Hot Line was founded at the start of the Korean women's movement. It runs counseling centres and shelters for survivors of domestic and sexual violence but describes itself as a movement organization, closer in spirit to Taiwan's Awakening Foundation than to a service provider.

Thailand, 1990. Researchers and activists in Bangkok launched ECPAT (End Child Prostitution in Asian Tourism) as a three-year campaign against child sex tourism. It grew into a global network of more than a hundred member organizations, and in 1996 it co-organized the first World Congress against the Commercial Sexual Exploitation of Children in Stockholm.

blocks.text: The comparison shows two paths. Some groups stayed small and political, while others, like Garden of Hope and HELP, became service institutions that depend on government contracts. Both paths are legitimate, but they suit different kinds of partnership. A movement group may welcome money for campaigns, while a service provider can show you exactly how many shelter nights a donation paid for.

sections.title: Garden of Hope as a possible partner

blocks.text: Here is a plain summary of what this lesson suggests about Garden of Hope as a cool dairy partner.

items: Strengths: a thirty-eight-year record, national reach, audited accounts, detailed public reports, and services such as shelters and job training whose results can be counted.

Things to weigh: its scale means a small shop's donation would be a very small share of its NT$270 million in annual donations, so the story you can tell customers will be about joining a large effort rather than funding something new. Its Christian identity and its position against legalizing prostitution may or may not match cool dairy's values.

Questions to ask: Is there a specific project, such as the economic empowerment programme or the girls' homes, that a donation can be earmarked for? Will the donation be listed in the published donor records? Does it already have a secondhand or resale partnership model? It runs material-donation drives and its own shops, so a clothing link may be natural.

sections.title: A question to take with you

blocks.text: Garden of Hope gets about 48 percent of its income from government contracts and 42 percent from donations. Would you rather cool dairy's money go to a large, government-funded service provider whose results are easy to measure, or to a smaller movement organization like the Awakening Foundation, where a small donation matters more but the results are harder to count? What would you want to tell customers in each case?

fun_fact.title: Daisies instead of child prostitutes
fun_fact.text: Garden of Hope uses the daisy, 雛菊, as its symbol for protecting children. The choice is a pointed piece of wordplay: the old word for a child prostitute, 雛妓, shares the same first character 雛, meaning a young bird or a young girl. In 2025, the thirtieth anniversary of the 1995 law, the Ministry of Health and Welfare held an exhibition about the fight against child sexual exploitation called 「向陽雛菊」, 'daisies turned toward the sun', and Garden of Hope took part.

glossary.explain: 勵馨社會福利事業基金會, a Christian-rooted foundation founded in 1988 that began with a halfway house for girls rescued from prostitution and now provides services against gender-based violence across Taiwan.
A street in Taipei's Wanhua district, a well-known red-light area in the 1980s. Marches there on 10 January 1987 and 9 January 1988 protested child prostitution.
A Presbyterian Church in Taiwan project started in 1986 by Liao Pi-ying to rescue girls, many of them Indigenous, from child prostitution.
Head of the Presbyterian Church in Taiwan's Rainbow women's ministry centre in the 1980s; she investigated child prostitution, began the Rainbow Project and co-convened the Huaxi Street marches.
A co-convener of the Huaxi Street marches and a co-founder of the Taiwan Women's Rescue Association in 1987.
Secretary-general of the Awakening Foundation in the late 1980s and a co-convener of the Huaxi Street marches.
An Atayal activist (born 1951, former Chinese name 陳金水) of the Alliance of Taiwan Aborigines, who was street commander of the 1987 and 1988 Huaxi Street marches and later a legislator.
A group founded in August 1987 by Tsao Ai-lan, Shen Mei-chen, Liao Pi-ying and others to combine feminist advocacy with rescue work; it later became the Taipei Women's Rescue Foundation (婦女救援基金會).
Taiwan's best-known feminist advocacy group, which grew out of Awakening magazine (1982) and became a foundation in 1987. It focuses on law reform rather than direct services.
The American missionary named by Chinese Wikipedia as the founder of Garden of Hope in 1988.
Garden of Hope's first halfway house, which the foundation describes as Taiwan's first halfway house for girls.
A residential home where people leaving a crisis, here girls rescued from prostitution, live with support until they can live independently.
A former chief executive of Garden of Hope, who wrote publicly against putting same-sex issues to a referendum.
Garden of Hope's chief executive since 2020; she joined in 1990 as a social worker at its halfway house.

glossary.term: Child and Youth Sexual Transaction Prevention Act
aliases: 兒童及少年性交易防制條例
glossary.explain: A law promulgated on 11 August 1995 to punish the buying and trafficking of minors for sex and to protect victims; Garden of Hope helped draft and lobby for it.

glossary.term: Child and Youth Sexual Exploitation Prevention Act
aliases: 兒童及少年性剝削防制條例
glossary.explain: The new name and text of the 1995 act, promulgated on 4 February 2015 and in force from 1 January 2017, covering sexual images and online exploitation as well as prostitution.
Garden of Hope's counseling centre for survivors of sexual assault and the people close to them, opened in its 1995–2001 stage.
A regional network of women's shelters that Garden of Hope says it helped call together in its 'gender justice' stage after 2008.
A Garden of Hope social enterprise opened in 2009 that trains and employs women leaving violence.
A business run mainly for a social goal, such as training or employing a disadvantaged group, rather than for profit for owners.
Violence directed at people because of their gender or that affects one gender disproportionately, including domestic violence, sexual violence, stalking and trafficking.

glossary.term: Charity Donations Destined for Public Welfare Act
glossary.explain: Taiwan's 2006 law on public fundraising appeals: who may run them, permits, receipts, a cap on fundraising costs, and public reports on what was raised and how it was spent.
Taiwan's 2018 law on foundations, in force from February 2019, covering governance, boards, accounting, audits and mandatory public disclosure.
In Taiwanese law, a private legal person formed when donors set aside property for a public-interest purpose, approved by a regulator and registered with a court.
Public verification of donations: a charity publishes who gave, how much, and how the money was used, so donors can check.
Taiwan's central ministry responsible for social welfare, protective services and charity fundraising permits.
A 2016 labour-law change giving workers one fixed day off and one flexible rest day each week; it raised staffing costs for shelters and other round-the-clock services.
A Taiwanese law in force since 2022 against stalking; Garden of Hope wants it widened and an emergency protection order added.
The movement in which survivors publicly name sexual harassment and assault. Taiwan had a major #MeToo wave in 2023.
The emergency rule imposed on Taiwan from 1949 to July 1987, which banned new parties and restricted protest and the press.
A December 1979 human-rights rally in Kaohsiung that ended in clashes; opposition leaders including Annette Lu were arrested and tried in military court.
The writer who introduced 'New Feminism' to Taiwan in the 1970s, was jailed after the Kaohsiung Incident, and became vice president in 2000.
A Tokyo shelter founded in 1986 by the Japan Woman's Christian Temperance Union, mainly for foreign women who were trafficking victims, and later for women and children of any nationality.
A Japanese Christian women's organization founded in 1886 that campaigned against licensed prostitution and opened the HELP shelter on its centenary.
A South Korean women's movement organization founded in 1983 that runs counseling centres and shelters for survivors of domestic and sexual violence.

aliases: End Child Prostitution in Asian Tourism
glossary.explain: A campaign launched in Bangkok in 1990 against child sex tourism, now a global network of more than a hundred member organizations working against the sexual exploitation of children.

glossary.term: World Congress against the Commercial Sexual Exploitation of Children
glossary.explain: The first global conference on the sexual exploitation of children, held in Stockholm in 1996 and co-organized by ECPAT, UNICEF and an NGO group.
Money a charity receives from government, either as grants or as payment for services the government has contracted it to provide, such as running shelters.
Spending on running the organization itself, such as finance, IT, management and training, rather than on direct services.
Daisy; Garden of Hope's symbol for protecting children, a play on 雛妓, the old word for a child prostitute.
Huiru's planned vintage clothing shop whose proceeds will go to Taiwan women's organizations.
The foundation that grew out of the Taiwan Women's Rescue Association; it works on gender violence and is known for its campaign for Taiwan's comfort women.

aliases: 台灣原住民族權利促進會
glossary.explain: An Indigenous rights organization founded in the 1980s that campaigned for land rights, name rights and against the trafficking of Indigenous girls.
A famous temple in Taipei's Wanhua district, next to Huaxi Street, where the 1987 march gathered.
